questions.stem: When does DNA replication occur in the cell cycle?

options.text: During prophase of mitosis
During anaphase of mitosis
During the S phase of interphase
During cytokinesis

questions.explanation: DNA replication occurs during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, BEFORE mitosis or meiosis begins. This is one of the most common misconceptions — many students incorrectly think DNA replication happens during prophase. By the time prophase starts, all DNA has already been replicated.

questions.stem: Is interphase a 'resting phase' of the cell cycle?

options.text: No — the cell is highly active during interphase, carrying out DNA replication, protein synthesis, and organelle duplication
No — but only because the cell is dividing during interphase
Yes — interphase is when the cell sleeps
Yes — the cell is inactive during interphase

questions.explanation: Interphase is NOT a resting phase. The cell is extremely active: during G1 it grows and carries out normal functions, during S phase it replicates all its DNA, and during G2 it continues to grow and prepares for division (synthesising proteins needed for mitosis). The cell spends most of its life in interphase.

questions.stem: How many daughter cells does mitosis produce, and are they diploid or haploid?

options.text: 4 genetically identical diploid cells
4 haploid cells
2 genetically different haploid cells
2 genetically identical diploid cells

questions.explanation: Mitosis produces 2 genetically identical diploid daughter cells (clones of the parent cell). MEIOSIS produces 4 genetically different haploid cells. This is a fundamental distinction. Mitosis is for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction. Meiosis is for producing gametes.

questions.stem: How many daughter cells does meiosis produce, and are they diploid or haploid?

options.text: 4 genetically different haploid cells
2 haploid cells
2 diploid cells
4 genetically identical diploid cells

questions.explanation: Meiosis produces 4 genetically different haploid cells (gametes). The chromosome number is halved (diploid → haploid), and genetic variation is introduced through crossing over and independent assortment. This ensures that when two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the diploid number is restored.

questions.stem: Does a chromosome always consist of two chromatids?

options.text: No — chromosomes never have chromatids
No — a chromosome only has two sister chromatids after DNA replication in S phase; before replication, it is a single chromatid
Yes — chromosomes always have two chromatids
Yes — but only in plant cells

questions.explanation: A chromosome consists of two sister chromatids (joined at the centromere) only AFTER DNA replication in S phase. Before replication, each chromosome is a single DNA molecule (one chromatid). After mitosis separates the chromatids, each daughter cell has single-chromatid chromosomes again.

questions.stem: During which stage of meiosis does crossing over occur?

options.text: Metaphase I of meiosis
Anaphase II of meiosis
Prophase of mitosis
Prophase I of meiosis

questions.explanation: Crossing over occurs during prophase I of meiosis, when homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) and exchange segments of DNA. This creates new combinations of alleles on the chromatids, increasing genetic variation. Crossing over does NOT occur during mitosis.

questions.stem: What is the difference between homologous chromosomes and sister chromatids?

options.text: Homologous chromosomes are found in haploid cells; sister chromatids are found in diploid cells
Sister chromatids come from different parents; homologous chromosomes are identical copies
Homologous chromosomes are a pair (one from each parent) with the same genes but potentially different alleles; sister chromatids are identical copies of one chromosome joined at the centromere
They are the same thing

questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes are a pair of chromosomes (one inherited from each parent) that have the same genes at the same loci but may carry different alleles. Sister chromatids are two identical copies of a single chromosome, produced during DNA replication and joined at the centromere.

questions.stem: At which stage of meiosis is the chromosome number halved?

options.text: During anaphase II, when sister chromatids are separated
During prophase I
During anaphase I, when homologous pairs are separated
During telophase II

questions.explanation: The chromosome number is halved during anaphase I of meiosis, when homologous chromosome pairs are pulled to opposite poles of the cell. This is called the reduction division. In anaphase II, sister chromatids separate (similar to mitosis), but the chromosome number stays the same (already haploid).

questions.stem: What are the three main sources of genetic variation in meiosis?

options.text: Transcription, translation, and replication
Mutation, DNA replication, and mitosis
Crossing over, independent assortment, and random fertilisation
Mitosis, binary fission, and budding

questions.explanation: The three main sources of genetic variation during sexual reproduction are: (1) crossing over during prophase I (exchange of DNA between homologous chromosomes), (2) independent assortment during metaphase I (random orientation of homologous pairs), and (3) random fertilisation (any sperm can fuse with any egg).

questions.stem: What is independent assortment?

options.text: The random distribution of mutations along a chromosome
The random orientation of homologous chromosome pairs at the metaphase plate during meiosis I, leading to different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in gametes
The separation of sister chromatids during mitosis
The process of DNA replication before cell division

questions.explanation: Independent assortment occurs during metaphase I of meiosis. Each pair of homologous chromosomes lines up randomly at the cell equator, independent of other pairs. This means the maternal and paternal chromosomes are distributed randomly into gametes. In humans (23 pairs), this gives 2²³ = over 8 million possible combinations.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of stages in mitosis?

options.text: Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase
Metaphase → Prophase → Telophase → Anaphase
Anaphase → Prophase → Metaphase → Telophase
Telophase → Anaphase → Metaphase → Prophase

questions.explanation: The correct order is PMAT: Prophase (chromosomes condense, nuclear envelope breaks down), Metaphase (chromosomes line up at the equator), Anaphase (sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite poles), Telophase (nuclear envelopes reform, chromosomes decondense). This is followed by cytokinesis.

questions.stem: What happens during anaphase of mitosis?

options.text: Chromosomes condense and become visible
Chromosomes line up at the cell equator
The nuclear envelope reforms
Sister chromatids are separated and pulled to opposite poles by spindle fibres

questions.explanation: During anaphase, the centromeres split and spindle fibres shorten, pulling the sister chromatids apart to opposite poles of the cell. Each chromatid is now considered an individual chromosome. In mitosis, this maintains the diploid chromosome number in both daughter cells.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of mitosis?

options.text: To halve the chromosome number
Growth, repair of damaged tissues, and asexual reproduction
To produce gametes for sexual reproduction
To create genetic variation in offspring

questions.explanation: Mitosis is used for growth (producing new cells for a growing organism), repair (replacing damaged or dead cells), and asexual reproduction (producing genetically identical offspring, e.g., in bacteria, plants via vegetative propagation). It produces genetically identical cells and maintains the chromosome number.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of meiosis?

options.text: To repair damaged DNA
To produce genetically different haploid gametes for sexual reproduction
To produce identical copies of cells
Growth and repair of tissues

questions.explanation: Meiosis produces haploid gametes (sex cells) that are genetically different from each other and from the parent cell. When two gametes fuse during fertilisation, the diploid number is restored. Meiosis introduces genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment.

questions.stem: Does crossing over occur during mitosis?

options.text: No — crossing over only occurs during prophase I of meiosis, when homologous chromosomes pair up
Yes — but only in plant cells during mitosis
No — crossing over only occurs during anaphase II
Yes — crossing over occurs in all cell divisions

questions.explanation: Crossing over does NOT occur during mitosis. It only occurs during prophase I of meiosis, when homologous chromosomes form bivalents and exchange segments of DNA at chiasmata. In mitosis, homologous chromosomes do not pair up, so there is no opportunity for crossing over.

questions.stem: What is cancer in terms of cell division?

options.text: Uncontrolled cell division caused by mutations in genes that regulate the cell cycle
A type of cell death
Cells dividing too slowly
Cells that have stopped dividing permanently

questions.explanation: Cancer results from mutations in genes that control the cell cycle, particularly proto-oncogenes (which become oncogenes, promoting division) and tumour suppressor genes (which normally inhibit division). These mutations cause cells to divide uncontrollably, forming tumours.

questions.stem: What are stem cells?

options.text: Dead cells that form the stem of a plant
Cells that have already fully differentiated into a specific cell type
Undifferentiated cells that can divide and differentiate into specialised cell types
Cells that can only produce more stem cells

questions.explanation: Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that have the ability to divide by mitosis and differentiate into specialised cell types. Embryonic stem cells can become any cell type (pluripotent), while adult stem cells are more limited (multipotent). Stem cells are important in growth, repair, and medical research.

questions.stem: What happens during prophase of mitosis?

options.text: Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles
Chromosomes condense, spindle fibres form, and the nuclear envelope breaks down
DNA replication occurs
The cell plate forms between the two new cells

questions.explanation: During prophase: chromosomes condense and become visible, the spindle apparatus forms from centrioles, and the nuclear envelope breaks down. The chromosomes (each consisting of two sister chromatids) become shorter and thicker. DNA replication has already occurred during S phase of interphase.

questions.stem: What happens during metaphase of mitosis?

options.text: Homologous chromosomes pair up
Chromosomes condense and become visible
Individual chromosomes line up along the cell equator (metaphase plate), attached to spindle fibres at their centromeres
The nuclear envelope reforms

questions.explanation: During metaphase, chromosomes line up individually along the cell equator (metaphase plate). Spindle fibres from opposite poles attach to the centromere of each chromosome. In mitosis, individual chromosomes line up. In meiosis I, homologous PAIRS line up (this is independent assortment).

questions.stem: What is cytokinesis?

options.text: The condensation of chromosomes
The replication of DNA
The separation of sister chromatids
The division of the cytoplasm to form two separate daughter cells

questions.explanation: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm, which occurs after mitosis (nuclear division) to produce two separate daughter cells. In animal cells, a cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two. In plant cells, a cell plate forms between the two new cells, which develops into a new cell wall.

questions.stem: How does cytokinesis differ between plant and animal cells?

options.text: There is no difference — it occurs the same way in both
Animal cells form a cleavage furrow that pinches inward; plant cells form a cell plate that grows outward
Plant cells use a cleavage furrow; animal cells form a cell plate
Only animal cells undergo cytokinesis; plant cells do not

questions.explanation: In animal cells, a ring of contractile proteins (actin and myosin) forms a cleavage furrow that pinches the cell inward until it splits in two. In plant cells, the rigid cell wall prevents pinching, so vesicles fuse to form a cell plate in the middle, which develops into a new cell wall separating the daughter cells.

questions.stem: What are the phases of interphase?

options.text: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase
Interphase has no distinct phases
G1 (growth), S (DNA synthesis), G2 (preparation for division)

questions.explanation: Interphase consists of three phases: G1 (Gap 1) — the cell grows, carries out normal functions, and prepares for DNA replication; S (Synthesis) — DNA is replicated; G2 (Gap 2) — the cell continues to grow and synthesises proteins needed for cell division (e.g., tubulin for spindle fibres).

questions.stem: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will be in a gamete after meiosis?
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number (diploid → haploid). A human body cell has 46 chromosomes (2n = 46), so after meiosis, each gamete has 23 chromosomes (n = 23). When two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the diploid number (46) is restored in the zygote.

questions.stem: In humans, how many different chromosome combinations are possible from independent assortment alone?

options.text: Over 8 million (2²³)
Exactly 100

questions.explanation: In humans, there are 23 pairs of homologous chromosomes. During meiosis I, each pair can orient independently, giving 2²³ = 8,388,608 possible combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in the gametes. Combined with crossing over and random fertilisation, the number of genetically unique offspring is essentially infinite.

questions.stem: Why does mitosis NOT produce genetic variation?

options.text: Because mitosis only occurs in haploid cells
Because mitosis does not involve DNA
Because mutations never occur during mitosis
Because homologous chromosomes do not pair up, there is no crossing over, and there is no independent assortment — daughter cells are genetically identical to the parent

questions.explanation: Mitosis does not produce genetic variation because: (1) homologous chromosomes do not pair up (no bivalents), (2) there is no crossing over, (3) chromosomes line up individually (no independent assortment of homologous pairs), and (4) sister chromatids are genetically identical. The daughter cells are clones of the parent cell.

questions.stem: What is a bivalent (tetrad)?

options.text: A pair of sister chromatids
A pair of homologous chromosomes that have come together during prophase I of meiosis, consisting of four chromatids
A cell with four sets of chromosomes
A chromosome that has not replicated

questions.explanation: A bivalent (also called a tetrad) is formed when two homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) during prophase I of meiosis. Since each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids, a bivalent contains four chromatids in total. This is when crossing over can occur between non-sister chromatids.

questions.stem: What is a chiasma (plural: chiasmata)?

options.text: The centromere of a chromosome
The point where non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes cross over and exchange DNA segments during prophase I
The cell equator where chromosomes line up during metaphase
The point where a chromosome is attached to a spindle fibre

questions.explanation: A chiasma is the physical point of contact where non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes have crossed over and exchanged segments of DNA. Chiasmata are visible during prophase I of meiosis and are evidence that crossing over has occurred, creating recombinant chromatids.

questions.stem: After crossing over in meiosis, are sister chromatids still identical?

options.text: No — crossing over exchanges DNA segments between non-sister chromatids, so the sister chromatids may now carry different alleles
No — but only if a mutation has also occurred
Yes — only the homologous chromosomes are changed
Yes — crossing over does not change the chromatids

questions.explanation: After crossing over, sister chromatids may no longer be identical because sections of DNA have been exchanged between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. This means each of the four chromatids in a bivalent may carry a unique combination of alleles, increasing genetic variation.

questions.stem: What is differentiation?

options.text: The process by which a cell dies
The process by which a cell divides into two identical cells
The process by which DNA is replicated
The process by which a cell becomes specialised for a particular function by expressing specific genes

questions.explanation: Differentiation is the process by which an unspecialised cell becomes specialised for a particular function. This involves specific genes being switched on or off, producing specific proteins that give the cell its unique structure and function. For example, a stem cell can differentiate into a nerve cell, muscle cell, etc.

questions.stem: What is the difference between meiosis I and meiosis II?

options.text: There is no difference — they are identical processes
Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes (reduction division); meiosis II separates sister chromatids (similar to mitosis)
Meiosis I separates sister chromatids; meiosis II separates homologous chromosomes
DNA replication occurs between meiosis I and meiosis II

questions.explanation: Meiosis I is the reduction division — homologous chromosome pairs are separated, halving the chromosome number from diploid to haploid. Meiosis II is similar to mitosis — sister chromatids are separated. Importantly, there is NO DNA replication between meiosis I and meiosis II.

questions.stem: A cell has 8 chromosomes (2n = 8). After meiosis I, how many chromosomes does each cell have?

options.text: 4 (each with two chromatids)
8 (each with two chromatids)
4 (each with one chromatid)

questions.explanation: After meiosis I, each cell has half the original number of chromosomes: 4 chromosomes (the haploid number). Each chromosome still consists of two sister chromatids (joined at the centromere) because meiosis I separates homologous pairs, not sister chromatids. Sister chromatids are separated in meiosis II.

questions.stem: What role do spindle fibres play in cell division?

options.text: They form the cell plate in plant cells
They attach to chromosomes at the centromere and pull them to opposite poles of the cell
They break down the nuclear envelope
They replicate DNA

questions.explanation: Spindle fibres (microtubules) are formed from centrioles and attach to chromosomes at the centromere via kinetochores. During anaphase, the spindle fibres shorten, pulling sister chromatids (mitosis/meiosis II) or homologous chromosomes (meiosis I) to opposite poles of the cell.

questions.stem: What is the significance of maintaining chromosome number during mitosis?

options.text: It is not significant — chromosome number can vary between cells
It ensures all body cells have the same complete set of genetic information needed for normal function
It prevents mutations from occurring
It allows cells to reproduce sexually

questions.explanation: Maintaining the chromosome number during mitosis ensures every body (somatic) cell has a complete and identical copy of the organism's genetic information. This is essential for all cells to function correctly. If chromosome number changed during mitosis, cells would have missing or extra genes, causing abnormalities.

questions.stem: What is non-disjunction?

options.text: The crossing over of chromosomes during prophase I
The failure of chromosomes to separate properly during meiosis, resulting in gametes with too many or too few chromosomes
The normal separation of chromosomes during cell division
The pairing of homologous chromosomes

questions.explanation: Non-disjunction is the failure of homologous chromosomes (in meiosis I) or sister chromatids (in meiosis II) to separate properly. This results in gametes with an extra chromosome or a missing chromosome. For example, non-disjunction of chromosome 21 can lead to Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

questions.stem: What happens during telophase of mitosis?

options.text: Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles
Chromosomes condense and become visible
Nuclear envelopes reform around each set of chromosomes, and the chromosomes begin to decondense
Chromosomes line up at the cell equator

questions.explanation: During telophase, the separated chromosomes arrive at opposite poles, nuclear envelopes reform around each group of chromosomes, and the chromosomes begin to decondense (uncoil). This is essentially the reverse of prophase. Cytokinesis (division of the cytoplasm) then follows to complete cell division.
